questions.q: What does "least privilege" mean, precisely, per this lesson?
options: A role's policy grants exactly the actions, on exactly the resources, that the workload needs — nothing broader just in case
Every role should be granted full administrator access by default for simplicity
Only the root account should ever be used to run pipelines
Policies should never specify a Resource field at all
questions.explain: Least privilege is a concrete scoping discipline, not a vague aspiration — it shows up directly in the Action and Resource fields.

questions.q: Why is {"Action": "s3:*", "Resource": "*"} a least-privilege violation even if the role only ever calls s3:GetObject?
options: Because the grant is far broader than what's actually used — it allows every S3 action on every bucket, creating unnecessary blast radius if the role is ever compromised
Because that policy syntax is technically invalid and won't work
Because AWS charges extra for wildcard actions
It isn't a violation — matching actual usage doesn't matter, only whether the policy runs
questions.explain: Least privilege cares about the maximum a policy grants, not just what the workload happens to use — the gap is the risk.

questions.q: Per this lesson's example, what is scoped differently between the ingestion Lambda, the Glue transform job, and the analyst's read-only role?
options: Each gets a different slice of buckets, prefixes, and actions matched to exactly what that specific job touches
All three are granted identical, unrestricted S3 access for consistency
Only the analyst's role is allowed to touch S3 at all
They are scoped by AWS Region only, with identical actions and resources otherwise
questions.explain: The ingestion Lambda can't read the curated bucket at all — each role's grant matches its actual job, nothing shared unnecessarily.

questions.q: What is the practical workflow this lesson recommends for scoping a new pipeline role's permissions?
options: Grant the smallest set of actions you're confident it needs, run it, use CloudTrail to see what was denied, then add exactly that
Start with full administrator access and never narrow it down
Grant Resource "*" permanently since resource-level scoping is never supported
Guess permissions once and never revisit them regardless of errors
questions.explain: Start narrow, observe real denials via CloudTrail, and widen only with evidence — the opposite of the far more common start-too-broad failure mode.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is every use of "Resource": "*" automatically a mistake?
options: No — some older or broader API actions genuinely don't support resource-level scoping and require a wildcard; that's a real constraint, not laziness
Yes, every single API action in AWS supports resource-level scoping with no exceptions
Yes, and any policy using it should always be rejected outright
The lesson does not address this question at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes some actions require a wildcard due to real service constraints — worth distinguishing from careless over-granting.
